solutions.check: 26 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Time's against Brown, lacking Washington's lead — "I most upset a player"

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and thrown into disorder, so the letters are rearranged
lacking means going without, so that letter is dropped from the surname

parts.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time
Gordon Brown, the former prime minister

indicators.note: the lead of a name is the letter at its front

explanation.surface: A political quote: time is running out for Gordon Brown, and someone confesses to having upset a musician.
explanation.walkthrough: T sits against (next to) the rest; Brown without its W joins I MOST, and the whole lot is shuffled into TROMBONIST.
explanation.definitionFit: A trombonist is a musician who plays the trombone, so is a player in a band or orchestra.

clue.text: Two ways Cameron familiarly stands up and ducks the question?

indicators.note: in a down clue, standing up means being read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: two compass directions, south and east
the familiar short form of David Cameron's first name

explanation.surface: David Cameron, standing up at the despatch box, dodges a question in two different ways.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole string SE + DAVE is read upwards, giving EVADES.
explanation.definitionFit: To evade is to sidestep or avoid, which is what a politician who ducks the question does.

clue.text: Insistent type, Bill, when straddling Lewinsky's head

indicators.note: straddling means having a leg on each side, so one word sits around the other

parts.note: a bill is a posted notice or label, like a sticker

indicators.note: the head of a name is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A saucy picture of Bill Clinton and Monica Lewinsky, with an insistent type thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like Clinton, but it is a poster or label; Lewinsky's head is just her initial.
explanation.definitionFit: A stickler is someone who insists on exactness or on a particular rule being followed.

clue.text: "End of Obama!" — tabloid gets embarrassed retraction axed?

definitions.note: an adjective for something chopped up; the answer is an adverb meaning into pieces

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: The Sun, the British tabloid newspaper

indicators.note: a retraction draws something back, so the word for embarrassed is read backwards

parts.note: red in the face with embarrassment

explanation.surface: A tabloid headline cheering the end of Obama, then an embarrassing retraction gets spiked.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid daily. The question mark flags that the definition is loose: something axed is torn asunder.
explanation.definitionFit: Asunder means apart or into pieces, the state of something chopped up with an axe.

clue.text: Not without purpose, having what it takes to go after Bush's guts

indicators.note: going after means following, so this piece comes second in the answer
the guts of a word are its inner letters

explanation.surface: Someone with a purpose who has what it takes to go after George Bush.
explanation.definitionFit: Something usable can serve a purpose, so it is not without use or function.

clue.text: Begs Brown to reverse new role (is on the outside)

indicators.note: being on the outside means wrapping round everything else
reverse means turn round, so the title is read backwards

parts.note: Gordon Brown was Prime Minister, PM

indicators.note: new means made afresh, so the letters are rearranged into a fresh order

explanation.surface: Someone begs Gordon Brown to change course and take on a new role while out of power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is on the outside' sounds like Brown out in the cold; it tells you IS wraps the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To implore is to beg or plead earnestly, so implores is a straight synonym of begs.

clue.text: (& 23dn.) Crappy beer given to the underprivileged

parts.note: vulgar British slang for weak beer

explanation.surface: Lousy beer handed out to the needy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crappy beer' reads as one phrase, but the definition is just 'Crappy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Piss-poor is coarse British slang for extremely bad or of very low quality.

clue.text: Churchmen against replacing first of medieval organs

indicators.note: replacing means taking the place of one letter with another
the first of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: Senior clergy set against the replacement of medieval church organs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organs' looks like church instruments, but means the genitals. V takes the place of M in PRIMATES.
explanation.definitionFit: Privates is a euphemism for the genitals, the private sexual organs.

clue.text: Climax of business exec. grabbing Mrs Mop's tops

indicators.note: grabbing means clutching hold, so one piece goes around the other

parts.note: a suit is slang for a business executive

indicators.note: the tops of words are their initial letters

parts.note: the first letters of Mrs and Mop

explanation.surface: A sleazy executive's climax comes from groping the cleaning lady.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Mop is an old British nickname for a cleaning woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A summit is the highest point or peak, so the climax of something.

clue.text: Rocky is clean-limbed, as featured in the Eye

indicators.note: rocky means unsteady and shaky, so the letters are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: Rocky Balboa, the boxer, looks lean and fit in the magazine's pages.
explanation.walkthrough: Rocky, the boxing film hero, would train with medicine balls, but here the name only signals the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Medicine Balls is the title of Private Eye's regular column on health and the NHS.

clue.text: Financier's first bad loss — "One must get stuck in, old thing!"

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter
getting stuck in means being lodged inside something else
bad means gone wrong, so the letters are out of their proper order

explanation.surface: A financier takes his first bad loss and someone tells the old fellow to knuckle down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old thing' sounds like a chummy address, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A fossil is the preserved remains of an ancient organism, and colloquially an old-fashioned person.

clue.text: Medicine makes the organ subside, getting small

parts.note: the eye is an organ of sight
S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A smutty picture of a drug that makes a certain organ go down and shrink.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface steers towards a different organ; the one wanted is the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Eye-drops are liquid medication applied to the eye a drop at a time.

clue.text: Palin's opening official address reveals what she covets?

indicators.note: the opening of a name is its initial letter

parts.note: an official residence, such as an ambassador's

explanation.surface: Sarah Palin's opening speech gives away her ambition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'official address' suggests a speech, but it is a home. Sarah Palin was the 2008 Republican vice-presidential candidate.
explanation.definitionFit: Palin was seen as wanting to be US president, so the presidency is the office she desired.

clue.text: Prince not right about off-colour Clinton?

indicators.note: about means around, so the name wraps around the other word
not means without, so that letter is removed from the name

explanation.surface: A gossipy question whether Prince Harry is wrong about a racy Clinton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off-colour' hints at a risqué Clinton but means unwell. The question mark shows Hillary is one example of a Clinton.
explanation.definitionFit: Hillary Clinton is a well-known bearer of the surname, so is one Clinton by example.

clue.text: Didn't put away all the chicken Labour party traditionalists?

definitions.text: Didn't put away all the chicken
definitions.meaning: first meaning: left a wing of the bird uneaten
second meaning: the socialist faction of the party

explanation.walkthrough: The first meaning is whimsical: someone who didn't finish the chicken left a wing on the plate.
explanation.definitionFit: The left wing of Labour is its more socialist, traditional faction, as opposed to modernisers.

clue.text: Pap producer after Sky's top dish

indicators.note: after means following, so the kitchen tool comes second
the top of a word is its first letter

parts.note: a masher turns food into pulp, or pap

explanation.surface: A kitchen tool for making mush, ranked as Sky's best dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dish' looks culinary, but it means an attractive person. Sky is a British satellite TV broadcaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Both smasher and dish are British slang for a very attractive person.

clue.text: Be a typical tabloid reporter? Male, screwed up — quite so!

indicators.note: something screwed up has been crumpled or botched, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A man made a mess of it, quite so: a dig at sloppy tabloid hacks.
explanation.definitionFit: To misquote is to report someone's words wrongly, a habit the clue jokingly pins on tabloid journalists.

clue.text: Say "love a tumble: it's good for one's self-esteem"

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: Advice that a romantic roll in the hay will boost your confidence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'love a tumble' reads as fancying a fling; a tumble is just a fall here.
explanation.definitionFit: An ego trip is an activity pursued mainly to boost one's own sense of importance.

clue.text: Having sex, whatsits in good

explanation.surface: Someone coyly avoids naming body parts while describing sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a container signal, but is just two letters in the line.
explanation.definitionFit: Stuffing is vulgar slang for having sexual intercourse.

clue.text: Elected king, ex-President loses lead in a sudden surge

indicators.note: losing the lead means the front letter falls away

explanation.surface: A crowned head is voted in while a former president falls behind in a sudden swing.
explanation.definitionFit: An inrush is a sudden flooding inward, a sudden surge of water, air or people.

clue.text: Sleazy bugger has way with Cyclops

indicators.note: has means holds within, so the insult holds the other letters

parts.note: British slang insult of the same strength
RD is the abbreviation for road
the setter speaking of himself, me, I

explanation.surface: A sleazy rogue gets his way with the setter.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves to clue I; here Cyclops, the setter's pseudonym, does it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sordid means dirty and morally squalid, so it is a synonym of sleazy.

clue.text: Eye shows cardinal, say, holding mock erection

indicators.note: holding means gripping within, so the colour surrounds the other word

parts.note: cardinal red, the colour of a cardinal's robes

indicators.note: an erection is a raising up, which in a down clue reads a word from the bottom

parts.note: to rag is to tease or mock

explanation.surface: A cardinal in the Eye's pages is caught in a mocked-up erection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eye' could be the magazine or the organ, but it is a verb, to look at.
explanation.definitionFit: To regard something is to look at it closely, which is what to eye it means.

clue.text: Might Labour, to reveal what undermined the Blair-Brown relationship?

parts.note: to labour is to toil or strive

explanation.surface: A wry look at the Labour Party, whose leaders fought each other for a decade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' looks like the party, but is the verb or noun for hard work. Blair and Brown were rival New Labour leaders.
explanation.definitionFit: The long contest between Tony Blair and Gordon Brown for control of the government was a power struggle.

clue.text: see 7dn.
They're rolled in in bits

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the next word goes within the other

explanation.surface: Cannabis cigarettes rolled up from bits and pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: The doubled 'in' looks like a typo: the first places the second inside JOTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Joints are cannabis cigarettes, which are hand-rolled.

clue.text: Work together? Clinton's guts react badly!

indicators.note: the guts of a word are its central letters
badly means wrongly, so the letters are put in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A gutsy jab at Bill Clinton reacting badly to a joint effort.
explanation.definitionFit: To interact is to act on each other, a loose sense of working together.
